154.Name: TSL
154.Story:
While his friends had often wondered why he didn't really resemble his parents, it wasn't until a group of the self-proclaimed Thorned Vengeance arrived at his house that Tamrus realized that something was wrong.
    It was the first time that his parents, always so loving and patiently responsive to his questions, actively avoided his querying eyes. They led the Thorned Vengeance into a room to talk quietly, the look in the latter's eyes as they swept past making Tamrus' skin crawl.
    It was not the first time these Thorned Vengeance had come to his village. They would look at him with the same loathing which plastered their faces as they ranted, spittle flying, about the evil committed by humans against the Wilders. Eventually, Tamrus was forced to face up to the fact that he was different from the others. He didn't have what other Wilders had: no tail, no claws. His large ears, of which he'd always been so proud, had even been made by his father. In fact, he appeared less like these forest companions and more like the humans the Thorned Vengeance railed against.
    He waited patiently until the Thorned Vengeance had left, then nervously asked his parents where he had really come from. Their reaction was not what he was expecting—they glanced at each other uneasily, but said not a word. A void seemed to open up inside him at their strange and unnatural expressions. Rubbing his large, drooping ears, he felt a stranger in his home for the first time in his life.
    Later, when his parents weren't looking, he snuck out of the house and wandered aimlessly in the forest.
    He stood atop a vast tree, wanting to gaze out over the vast arboreal sea as he usually did when troubled. But this time, his attention was immediately arrested by a whispered voice beneath him.
    "Get a move on, will you? We've still got another batch to hunt after this one's shipped off."
    Pushing aside the branches and leaves, Tamrus saw a group of humans, furtively hoisting dying animals onto their shoulders as they prepared to leave the Dark Forest. He followed the strangers, sneaking along the branches and trying to remain hidden amongst the leaves. Although his steps were light and nimble, the group seemed to notice slight movements and grew wary.
    "Watch yourselves now. We don't want those Thorned Vengeance finding us again." the human leader warned quietly.
    These must be the poachers the Thorned Vengeance always spoke about! He had to save the animals, but the poachers would get away if he went looking for help now. Tamrus frowned, thinking, then decided to stop them himself.
    He leapt nimbly from above, landing heavily right in the middle of the group. The shockwave generated by the impact disoriented those who managed to remain standing, as he yelled, "HEY! Who are you, and what do you think you're doing here?"
    "Uh... Isn't this a human kid?" One of the poachers suddenly exclaimed in surprise, looking closely at Tamrus. "What's a kid doing in the Dark Forest, dressed like that? And what's that on his head?!"
    "Hang on, you think this could be that baby Old Boozer threw into the forest?" Several of the poachers unconsciously dropped their guard at this, lowering their weapons and looking at each other before bursting into peals of laughter.
    "Hey, kid. Come here," the leader of the poachers coaxed, "I know some others around your age. They always have toys to play with and snacks to eat, and they don't run around the forest in rags like you. How about this—you tell us where the Wilders are, and we'll get you out of here, find your real parents. Whaddya say?"
    "That's right. Look at you, traipsing all over the forest like a savage, when the outside world is so much more exciting." another poacher agreed.
    "I'm not a savage!" Tamrus was furious, but quickly got his emotions under control and spoke again, as if suddenly thinking of something. "But I can take you. I know every inch of this place."
    "Just..." Tamrus squinted at them, "You'd better keep your word."

    He led them to a huge, dense thicket, saying that the Wilders he knew were behind it.
    "You wait here. I'll go get them to come out," Tamrus said, before disappearing into the middle of the thicket.
    Not long after a huge group of the Thorned Vengeance burst out in front of the expectant poachers, completely overpowering them before they could even react.
    Tamrus poked his head through the ring of Thorned Vengeance which surrounded them, smiling slyly, "I didn't lie to you! I told you I knew where the Wilders were!"
    While the leader of the Thorned Vengeance still had a sullen expression, he did look more gently upon Tamrus. Habitually taciturn, he merely nodded his appreciation at the child who had done them such a service. Tamrus suddenly felt a little embarrassed, but still raised his head high in response, his large ears shaking with pride.
    Right then, the fog which had been enveloping his mind was suddenly dispelled. Happily, Tamrus flew through the trees, his grappling hook whizzing through the air. He scampered homeward, bursting to tell his parents about his greatest ever achievement. But he didn't need to get that far because he bumped into his parents, anxiously out looking for him, while on the way.
    "My baby! We finally found you!" His mother hugged him close, plastering his face with kisses, guilt writ large on her own, "We just weren't ready to tell you before..."
    As his mother spoke, she reached out to wipe off some dirt from his face, her mind seeming to drift back in time. "It was many years ago... Your dad and I just found you, all alone in the forest, so—"
    "So you took me in!" Tamrus interrupted his mother, but the gentle eyes of her and his father gave him the courage to continue, "You watched me grow up. You are my only parents, and I will always be your son, and forever a child of the forest."

155.Name: DOA
155.Story:
An empire's path to glory is littered with the destroyed remnants of contenders. So it was with the Kingdom of Ozmanth, and Olgath the heir to its throne. There was indeed a time before the Lightbearer Empire dominated the lands of humanity with an iron fist—a time of brief heydays for humanity's lesser kingdoms before absorption into the behemoth of the empire. And so it was that the borders of the Lightbearer Empire encroached upon the otherwise peaceful kingdom of Ozmanth.
    The Lightbearer Empire sent envoys of peace, as always, to discuss the terms of their "new arrangement." The proposal? Incorporation into the empire as a somewhat autonomous duchy. For the empire this was already concession enough. Yet it was far from enough for Osmanth's king, Olgath's father, in recognizing the worth of that which his kingdom had built. He politely sent the emissaries away with eloquent words as to his hope of an enduring peace between their peoples. But the kindly words concealed a darker reality to the increasingly terrified subjects of Ozmanth: when a far mightier power seeks a "new arrangement," the terms of such an arrangement can be executed unilaterally. Rumors of a conflict with the mighty Lightbearers—or worse, war—drove the court into a panicked frenzy. There was already dissatisfaction with the king's rule. The fear of war added irresistible weight to forces calling for a change in government.
    It was Olgath's own uncle, General Roman, who ultimately plunged the dagger into his brother's back. He then naturally followed through with the execution of all other potential heirs within the family tree. His dagger reached far and wide, ultimately leaving only Olgath himself the sole survivor of his line. And what had the new king of Ozmanth gained for his treachery? An honorific position dependent entirely on his utter subservience to Ozmanth's new Lightbearer masters.
    Olgath survived. His sister almost survived. In fact, it was the bullet meant for Olgath that had left him severely wounded which killed his sister. She, like so many others loyal to the Palace, had died fighting the betrayer. Olgath fled, a shadow of his former self, his life's mission totally concerned only with revenge against Roman. But the boy had no army, not even the full functionality of his limbs. Crippled by the bullet that had killed his sister, Olgath was reduced to hunting for scraps in the ruins of border towns. On the rare occasion he encountered another living soul in the same predicament, he was often reduced to being shooed away like the helpless scavenger he now was. His waking life tortured him, and then his dreams tortured him again at night as he consistently beheld the same vision: a variation on his father and sister accusing him of failing to right the wrongs they had suffered, or the sight of Roman once again raising the barrel of a gun toward his family, who yet again fell to the ground lifeless. The details varied, but the theme remained. Olgath felt his mind splintering away into nothingness. And it was in the depths of absolute despair, when his soul was radiating the darkness of the Eternal Abyss, that he drew the attention of other, less natural creatures like a moth to a flame. And so it was that the Hypogeans came to Olgath's aid.
    The night had begun as any other with the same nightmare. But this night he did not dream alone. A slithering maggot-like creature twisted and crawled over the rubble, then climbed and slithered into the wound in the palm of his hand.
    The dream experienced an abrupt change of tone. Instead of Roman pointing the gun at his family and mowing them down like criminals, this time it was Olgath who blew Roman to smithereens—with nothing less than a powerful hand-held cannon shaped oddly like a maggot. Thereafter he began to dream that the cannon, or rather the maggot that had transformed itself into a cannon, was watching him intently. Some kind of spine-curdling fluid or emulsion sprang forth from the creature and enveloped Olgath within his dream. And then he began to hear strange whispers, barely yet somehow understood, that asked him whether he was willing to give everything he had to right the wrongs done to him.
    The next morning he awoke a changed man. He could scarcely believe what had happened overnight—his wounds, pain, and withered limbs were suddenly restored to their former vigor. Moreover, he was holding in his hand the same cannon that he had beheld in his dream. He was not just restored. Olgath had been given a power greater than his human body had originally possessed. It was most welcome, but like all Hypogean gifts were not for free—he would need to earn it through a sacrifice as bitter as his desire for revenge.
    And so Olgath the butcher was born that day. He quickly began his work of vengeance upon all those who had deprived him of his just desserts, starting with the annihilation by cannonfire of the other scavengers that had mocked him previously. Olgath emerged from the ruins a man triumphant, growing daily in added strength. With these newfound powers, all Olgath had to do was wait for the perfect moment to enact his revenge.
    Although just a figurehead, Duke Roman was still a well-guarded man. It took many moons for Olgath to locate his opportunity. The wretched traitor who had exchanged the lives of Olgath's family members for the comforts of a palatial estate was to attend the citywide celebrations as the guest of honor. The ideal moment to blast the duke would come during the cannon salute during the procession.
    The streets that day bustled with excited revelers. Olgath wasted no time appreciating the celebratory atmosphere. Instead he retreated to the shadows as his scowling thoughts turned to former days when he had attended the same event with his beloved family, not as an assassin. From the dark he gazed toward the likely point of arrival of the duke's grand procession. At last he saw Roman, his own uncle, the one who had stripped Olgath of all happiness in life, seated high upon the main carriage and waving with blissful ignorance at the crowd cheering with adulation. The sight was so disgusting to Olgath. He could think only of the bullet that had nearly lodged itself in his heart.
    Roman's procession neared. Olgath waited. The cannon salute began. There was an ear-splitting blast, so deafening only nearby onlookers noticed the shell aimed at the Duke's own entourage. There were screams. The crowd scattered. Olgath mowed down the last guards and then stood face-to-face with his arch-enemy. The terror on Roman's face was palpable. He began by pleading with Olgath to spare his life and launched into a long-winded explanation of why he had had no choice. Olgath paid him no heed. He pressed the barrel to the duke's temple—the better to give the duke an experience of what it means to know the minute of your own death.
    Olgath returned to his home among the ruins and kneeled down in exhaustion. His life's last wish had been granted. At the moment he had found ecstasy beyond comprehension, followed almost as quickly by a profound sense of emptiness. His body had also began to wither once again. Olgath began to think that perhaps his bargain with the Hypogean was done, who had now come to remove the unnatural vitality once granted. But Olgath's suspicions were too simplistic. A Hypogean could never be satisfied by the mere ruin of an individual soul. More would be required. Again Olgath heard the sweet, low murmur by his ear claiming Roman had been nothing but an insignificant pawn in the grand scheme of a much more evil empire. It was in fact the Lightbearer Empire Olgath should recognize as his true nemesis and author of all his woes. Olgath's despairing heart was quickened once again by the excitement of hatred. The Hypogean's poisoned words burrowed deep within his heart as the cannon began to pulsate with a new, disgusting fluid that spread down Olgath's arm and across his whole body. For this next task the Hypogean and Olgath must become one.
    Olgath stood up from his place among the ruins, tightly clutching a cannon within a barely-recognizable hand encased in bone. It was time to display the powers of this weapon to the whole Empire.
 
    "Cannon fire is a beautiful candle that flickers but for a moment. So is life."
155.DisplayTips: Ranger. Olgath deftly wields his cannon to scorch enemy formations, wreaking havoc with unique shells and powerful infernal shots.

156.Name: Adwin
156.Story:
Bantus' foreign wars never truly stopped. Even if they appeared to, it was merely to prepare for the next territorial expansion.
    Edwin had not long been of age when he voluntarily requested to go to the front line.
    The crown prince of Bantus at the time was his elder brother Thoran who, along with his dearly beloved sister Theowyn, was often consumed with worry over his safety. But Edwin was confident and driven, bringing necromancy to battlefields and countless victories back to the king. All would-be invaders were confined outside the Bantus borders by his Graveborn army.
    His outstanding military achievements and combat decorations made Edwin the youngest-ever general in the history of Bantus to score so many victories. The people called him the "Blade of Bantus," and he earned himself a seat on the prestigious political Council. Dignitaries from all over the land flocked to fawn at him and curry favor, thrusting him into the limelight.
    After sipping from the cup of such intoxicating power, Edwin dreamed of riding out at the head of his armored cavalry. His authority would be unquestioned, if he could bring all of Hathor under the dominion of Bantus.
    However, when the old, bellicose king died and Thoran ascended the throne, suddenly everything ran counter to his perfect vision of an imagined future.
    Edwin was officiating at a memorial to honor fallen warriors when a messenger burst in. He had come from the distant royal capital, thousands of leagues away, bearing the new king's declaration: Princess Theowyn was about to depart for Thalonia, a powerful nation on the western border, there to wed the crown prince. It was the king's sincere wish that border forces cease hostilities, and that the soldiers return to the royal capital to celebrate together with the nation.
    Edwin and the king had fallen out over just such a thing in the past. In his mind, the superiority of necromancy more or less assured the eventual domination of Bantus, so there was no need for the pampered princess to leave and get married. Attempting to make Thoran feel guilty, Edwin even abandoned his customary courtesy and brazenly questioned what their sister meant to him. But the king, always the soul of kindness, displayed nothing but an unusual indifference in the face of this question.
    "Years of constant war have brought myriad hidden dangers. Bantus needs a new path," Thoran said, "This is her inevitable sacrifice, and her duty, as a royal princess." 
    Faced with the king's unflinching attitude, Edwin could not object further. He knew well that only the power one held counted when making decisions.

    After the princess was married off to Thalonia, the relationship between the two countries gradually improved. This paved the way for the steady implementation of Thoran's future policies, and the influence of the pro-war faction waned day by day. After he abolished necromancy, which had done nothing but drag the people towards the abyss, the chorus of public praise and support swelled ever louder.
    But it was a slap in the face for Edwin.
    To neuter the country's greatest strength was like intentionally removing its armor and exposing its weak and vulnerable underbelly to all. Edwin was adamantly opposed while Thoran, always loving and indulgent of Edwin, was likewise adamant about enacting national policy changes. War and necromancy brought nothing but disaster and suffering to the people; only by pivoting to benevolence could the future of the kingdom be assured.
    He not only reprimanded Edwin publicly over his proposal to rearm the troops, but also ordered him to conduct a thorough self-reflection... while confined to the palace.
    Edwin, bereft of all support and authority, was enraged by this. Peace and national rejuvenation? Nothing but excuses, excuses that ignored the achievements of the living and trampled on the sacrifices of the dead. Only cowards dare utter such foolishness! If only he had the power of the throne, his counsellors would not have to abide by such incompetent decisions, his noble sister would not have to be offered up as some kind of sacrificial pawn, and his long-suffering people would not need to endure the shame of other countries invading their territory.
    Edwin was blinded by his resentment and rage. Thirsting for power, murderous intent soon arose in his frenzied heart.
    In order to seize all the power he envisaged, Edwin lured Theowyn back under the guise of asking her to mediate between himself and the king. But at the feast held to celebrate her homecoming, Thoran's death was the main course.
    Edwin felt no guilt as the tip of his sword pierced the chest of the king. Rather, he felt happier and freer than ever before. Finally, at long last, he had all of the Bantus in his grasp. All the criticism he had faced, all the humiliation, would vanish like smoke in the new dawn of a new regime. His regime...
    However, dessert had yet to be served, and the excitement was not yet over, as Edwin's life was also abruptly snuffed out.
    "Go to hell, you damn traitor!" 
    Thoran's devoted bodyguard, already slain, had become Graveborn under the power of necromancy. The sword he held skewered Edwin mercilessly from behind, before going on to slaughter all the traitors at the bloody banquet.
    Edwin fell to the ground, eyes wide in disbelief. He somehow still managed, before death claimed him, to stretch out one hand towards the fallen crown.

    The Lord of Fear never lets go of any resentful, unwilling soul. Inspired by the whispers of Quaedam, Edwin realized a new opportunity had been gained. While the coup had ended in the death of both king and rebels, Thoran was resurrected as the Fallen King by his most devoted and loyal servant, and under his brutal dictatorship Bantus became a kingdom of the dead.
    After Edwin was reborn, he stepped once again into the great hall. In the dim, flickering candlelight, the ruler of Bantus sat silent as a rock upon his throne, his loyal guards standing by with lowered eyes.
    Edwin touched one hand to his shoulder and bowed deeply to the ruler atop his dais. Hidden in the shadows, both his smile and his intention were unfathomable:
    "Shall we go on as we were, dearest brother?"

157.Name: BSparrow
157.Story:
"When darkness covers the world, the divine avians shall become the fiery salvation of all living things." Such are the great legends regarding the mythical "Obsidian Finches," a species only recorded in the most ancient of histories but which nonetheless once soared high above the skies of Esperia.
 
    It was in that ancient era that Maetria was born. From the time she first opened her eyes in her mother's nest, she had always held fast to the sacred mission told to her again and again by the eldest of the Obsidian Finches. Their sacred duty—the reason for their whole existence—was to protect Esperia.
 
    By the time of the great Elemental Strife that engulfed Esperia, Maetria's dedication to the mission of her race saw her rise to the position of chief over her people. She remembered keenly the words of her ancestors, and leapt into action to save the mortals scurrying fearfully about under their watchful eye. It was her burden, her duty, her honor, to play the role of savior.
 
    The Elemental Strife brought total calamity upon the helpless citizens of a frightened world. But it was nothing unexpected to Maetria and her folk. It was time for their mission to be fulfilled.
 
    Maetria honored all the old precepts taught to her and traveled deep into the Solaran Furnace. There, without reservation, she released the Solaris Flare that dwelled inside her. The ritual had begun. The burning Solaris Flare pierced the ground and lit up the sky in a magnificent display of celestial power, spreading across Esperia and cleansing it of all elemental disorder. Though Maetria felt the power being stripped from her body, she did not then lament the loss of her life, her mind filled only with joy at the glorious fulfilment of her mission. But this pride did not last long. She began to notice a new phenomenon; first with terror, then horror, and finally anger.
 
    She saw all her kinsfolk, all of the other Obsidian Finches, some of whom she had grown up with in the same nest, fall from the sky as the divine Solaris Flare within their bodies was ripped away. She watched them groan on the earth, dying, their feathers fading from brilliant red to gray and then finally ash as the life drained from their bodies. One hatchling Maetria knew well tried desperately to fly over for help. She was already a heap of ash by the time she landed at Maetria's feet.
 
    Maetria had been proud to do her part to save the world—the mission entrusted to her since birth. Yet no one had ever told her that saving the world would also come at the cost of her entire race.
 
    Maetria drew upon all the divine energy within her to try to halt the ritual, but there was nothing she could do. Virtually every member of her race was already dead or dying. Most cried out in pain as they faded to ash in front of her eyes. Maetria also sensed her own life force fading. It was then she came to the cruel realization that, in the end, all of the fanciful-sounding phrases about doing "what is best for Esperia" were nothing more than hollow lies to enable her species' exploitation. No! She resolved to herself. She would not give herself up in sacrifice, she would not die here! She vowed revenge on the world that had cruelly taken her kinsfolk away.
 
    Maetria's anger and desperate desire to save her species called out through the void to sinister forces like a beacon. Fell Hypogeans proffered a deal that Maetria quickly accepted: become their infernal vessel in exchange for unimaginable power. With the power to cheat death, she would live, and as long as she lived there was a hope of restoring her race, of reawakening them from the ash. She would stop at nothing to do so. Soon she emerged from the ash of her dying existence covered in dark flames— Hypogean flames.
 
    Maetria lay in wait for centuries, seeking some means by which the Obsidian Finches could be restored to life. And so passed a thousand years of futile searching, until finally she found the truth about her species' creation, as well as a way forward.
 
    Honas, the God of Creation, crafted the Furnace in the void when he made the world. From the sun he plucked a spark—called the "Solaris Flare"—and mixed it with the elemental forces to create Esperia. Yet a dark force of cosmic chaos had interfered with his great work. Hence, Esperia from its very inception possessed a slight imbalance between the elements, which would eventually culminate in disaster. It was a great defect in Honas' work, but he had a solution. He embedded his Furnace within the planet, in a place virtually undiscoverable. This became the "Solaran Furnace."
 
    Within the Furnace, Honas hid a special stone. Over the centuries, the stone would absorb the Solaran power and give birth to a race of divine avians—the Obsidian Finches.
 
    Eventually the disorder in Esperia's elemental forces culminated in the cataclysm once foretold. It was the Obsidian Finches, the carriers of the Solaris Flare, who were tasked with recreating the world without the imperfections in Honas' original work. Within the Furnace, the Obsidian Finches would have to release the Solaris Flare within themselves, allowing its divine power to spread across the land, seas, and skies. As the essence of their being, removing the Flare from the divine avians would result in their deaths. To protect Esperia with the Solaris Flare would be the glorious burden they would have to bear; yet to Maetria it seemed more a criminal's sentence. The Obsidian Finches were, in the end, no more than tools for correcting the Creator's mistakes, victims of his deceit. They were kindling to be burned.
 
    In this terrible truth, however, Maetria also uncovered a possible means to revive her kinfolk. There was still one Obsidian Finch left, and were the Elemental Strife to strike once more, she would only have to lead this last Finch to the Solaran Furnace. Using the remnants of the Solaris Flare within the last Finch, she could reignite the dormant Furnace and give her people a chance at rebirth.
 
    Maetria waited until a new Strife afflicted Esperia. Talene, the last Obsidian Finch, had made herself known, and within her dwelled the last vestiges of the Solaris Flare. By now, Maetria had waited for millennia, but the time had come for her plans to finally bear fruit. Taking on the guise of a Wilder scholar, she appeared before Talene when the time was right.
 
    "Honored Obsidian Finch, let me tell you a story of the divine avians of old..."

158.Name: Slacker
158.Story:
Dear sister,
 
    I'll try to make this brief. Please don't look for me anymore; you know as well as I do that no one can catch me unless I let it happen. By the time this letter reaches you, your baby should have been born; I wish your kid good health and a fulfilling childhood, the kind that we never had.
 
    Back when we were just a couple of starving orphans, it was Rodrey's father who took us off the streets and into his army. Only the strongest children could survive his training, only to become expendable soldiers for him, Anasta, the Quicksand Claws, and all of the Falkin. We swore to protect each other no matter what, but when I saw you at your wedding, and I saw the way you looked at Rodrey... I knew you had found your home, which meant that I had lost my own. Without my sister, I became a wanderer again.
 
    I have no right to complain; I was his best spy, after all. I killed in the darkness for him, and he conquered the land without mercy, leaving plenty of widows and orphans like us in his wake. A never-ending cycle of death... Do you remember Leah? I mentioned her to you before, which is something I rarely do; she's the one who likes to wear flowers on her head. We used to get paired up for missions all the time. We were scouting out an exile camp in the desert one night, and the stars were shining so bright in the sky.
 
    All of a sudden, she asked me, "What's going to happen to these exiles once we report their camp's location?"
 
    I told her that she already knew the answer, that Rodrey would trample this place into dust, just like he always has.
 
    Leah didn't say anything until morning... That's when she asked me if we could avoid telling Rodrey about the camp.
 
    Maybe she had recognized her old tribe? Or maybe she was just tired? I looked her straight in the eyes; according to Rodrey's laws, I should have killed her on the spot.
 
    But I didn't. Instead, I agreed with her.
 
    Leah was very happy after that. She said that even though we couldn't return to the tribe anymore, we could build ourselves a small hut at the edge of the Dark Forest. We wouldn't have to kill anymore, and we could work as bodyguards for traveling merchants to get by.
 
    The night after that, I fell into a heavy sleep and dreamed about the oasis where we were born. I wish I hadn't, because as soon as I opened my eyes... I saw them plunging a knife into Leah's back and stealing our food, the very same exiles we had just spared. She was planning to distribute that food to them in the morning. Leah looked at me with tears in her eyes as a gurgling noise came out of her throat; it felt like she was asking me to forgive her.
 
    The rest was history. Only a few exiles survived that night, and I buried Leah under that same, starry sky. Even though our mission was complete, I still didn't want to go back to the tribe; there was just no point in me being there anymore. They can call me whatever they want: a traitor, a deserter, a waste of Rodrey's manpower... But I refuse to hurt my former comrades anymore.
 
    With Dura's blessing, I'd like to go back and see the oasis of our births, or maybe the edge of the Dark Forest. I still haven't decided.
 
<r>So forgive me, and forget about me.</r>
<r>Crassio</r>

161.Name: DivineBlade
161.Story:
Athalia panted hard, more exhausted than she'd ever been before. The interior of the dilapidated church was covered in sword marks, a testament to her battle with the Hypogean leader before her. The keen blade she held was cracked and pitted all over, as was the armor she wore. 
 
    This particular Hypogean was not the strongest she had ever faced, but it was certainly the most troublesome, not to mention the fact that these lands, bordering the Lightbearer, were crawling with Hypogeans. She'd been fighting hordes of them almost daily, ever since she's first arrived here on the trail of that strange meteor. Days of fierce fighting had left her riddled with wounds and close to exhaustion.
 
    Behind Athalia, the refugees who had been subjected to the torments of the Hypogeans cowered beneath a statue of the goddess Dura. They had only just arrived to seek shelter at the only church in the desolate wilderness, to walk right into the middle of this terrible conflict. Wanting to flee, they had been paralyzed by the gaze of the Hypogean leader, and could only huddle under the statue, trembling and terrified of making a sound. It was as if they hoped to go unnoticed if only they shrank back even further.
 
    Athalia had long understood that was just how mortals were, cowardly and weak. She had once detested rebellious and ignorant mortals, but her opinion of them had changed over her years of wandering in the human world. It was as Dura had said: mortals did not possess divine power, and must therefore face difficulties no god need fear, such as disease, hunger, aging, and death...
 
    Athalia had traveled the world after the fall of the Dura. Her blade brings divine retribution to the heretical followers of the Hypogeans. She was both revered and feared by the people, who worshiped her as a god but secretly called her a merciless executioner, and avoided her in their fear.
 
    She had met many different types of humans over the years: veterans who bullied new recruits however they could; men who defended their border homeland alone, in the face of Mauler raiders; ferrymen who would stop in the middle of a river and extort higher fares; close friends who share their last sip of water while treasure hunting in the desert; young men, undercover in factions, feeding information about heresies back to the Temple of Light; single mothers who work three jobs, slaving away from morning to night...
 
    But humanity can never be so simply defined by good and evil. Just when you think you know someone's true character, they can often go against your expectations.
 
    The old veteran who protects the new recruit by blocking the enemy's sword with his own body; the lone man defending his home takes a mortal wound from behind; the ferryman uses his life savings to build a bridge over the river; the friends who shared their water ultimately fails to share the treasure; the targets in the young man's intelligence report were all outsiders; the daughter of the busy mother doesn't want to marry a rich businessman, yet is forced into a corner...
 
    Athalia gradually came to understand the teachings of the goddess:
 
    "The same person will kill when they are starving, yet care when they are sated. Humans are so complicated, you need to look at them from different perspectives."
 
    In reality, humans were even more complicated than Dura had said. Sometimes, both killing and caring were unconnected to hunger or satiety. Rich merchants who have all they could possibly need amass still more wealth by any means, while ordinary people, hungry and cold, could nevertheless show solicitude to total strangers.
 
    Despite being regarded as a ruthless god, Athalia had still experienced the kindness of humans on many occasions, who expected nothing in return.
 
    A destitute little girl thanked her with a handmade doll; a disabled blacksmith rescued her from the wilderness when she was seriously injured, and repaired her shattered blade with mortal iron... While these sorts of experience were infrequent, they gave her an inkling of something uniquely humane, something even the gods did not possess.
 
    In the past, she had a binary view of humans, they were either totally good or totally bad. She made her judgments with Hypogean corruption as the sole criterium, and executed justice on wicked heretics like a ruthless weapon. But humans cannot be so simply categorized. They often wavering between good and evil, and can fall into the darkness with but a single misstep.
 
    Thus she became a sharp sword hanging high above Esperia, hoping to prevent the scales of human hearts from too easily tipping over to the evil side. But for those who dared seek out the darkness of their own accord, never would her blade show the slightest hint of mercy. No longer was she just an unfeeling weapon, but a god who used her power more selectively when wielding her weapon.
 
    Inside the church Athalia was forced back by the Hypogean leader. Her blade, repaired by the blacksmith, shattered into pieces, and she could barely keep her feet. The Hypogean sneered malevolently at her, mocking her powerlessness. The timid mortals who prostrated themselves at the statue's foot would soon follow the Hypogeans, once Athalia died. It approached her step by step, preparing to bury a god.
 
    "Merciful Dura... Dispel fear and gloom from the world..." 
    "May the... Divine Light save these souls, tormented by the Hypogeans..."
 
    Quavering voices arose in the crowd as the refugees spontaneously began to pray, for themselves as well as for Athalia. Their voices became louder and firmer, the Hypogean's glare was now unable to quell them for even a moment. The trickle of prayer became a torrent which echoed throughout the church, suppressing even the mocking malevolence of the Hypogean.
 
    Perhaps the goddess had heeded the mortals' prayer, as Athalia's body began glowing with a faint incandescence. Light gathered, and condensed behind her into a shimmering blade, and an intense radiance surged out of her. Athalia rose into the air, bathed in light, her body transformed into a giant sword, the dazzling brilliance of which seemed to pierce the ceiling of the church.
 
    From the vault of heaven, down crashed the great sword.

162.Name: HammerMan
162.Story:
"Moltenflow soul burns in the heart, an endless road towards eternal spring. Over the majestic mountains, over the peaceful plains, the way home is near but yet so far."
     As the midnight bonfire burned ever fiercer, no one knew who first began to croon the old ballad. But one by one, the Dwarves who were deep in their cups began to join in the chorus. It was a well-known folksong which had become more popular in recent years, a song which sang of shameful days when the Dwarves were dependent, and their thirst to reclaim their homeland.
     Perhaps too absorbed in the song, the Dwarven chorus grew deeper and sadder, as if driven by sheer melancholy. However, just then another Dwarf, hitherto still busy with work, drew aside his tent flap and joined in.
     He took a half-spilled cup of bitter juice from the hands of a soldier who had passed out from exhaustion. Then his resonant voice boomed out, interrupting the half-finished song and startling all the Dwarves, lost as they were deep in memory.
     "Warriors! Raise your heads and your cups right this instant! Let us drain this bitter juice together, in praise of your courage! May your beards grow ever longer! And your hair, of course!"
     Loud laughter burst from the soldiers around the bonfire and reverberated through the valley. Their cups clashed together in time with the ballad, and their spoons banged out the rhythm on the side of the huge cooking pot.
     Sensing the atmosphere had lightened once more, the Dwarf was the first to drain the bitter juice he held. Then he went amongst the crowd, and made his way alone atop a boulder at their rear for a better view.
     This Dwarf, able to boost morale with but a few words, was none other than the commander of the famed Moltenflow Regiment. Young ones born after the outbreak of the second Hypogean war all grew up hearing about his exploits...
     Years ago, the Hypogeans who had overrun the mountains razed the Dwarven homeland. At that time of mortal peril, the Moltenflow Regiment had covered the safe retreat of the others, although they were almost wiped out in the process. But Ginneas, the sole survivor of the Moltenflow Regiment, fought his way out from the horde of encircling Hypogeans, together with the Frozen Mother.
     It would be a grave mistake to think that Ginneas' legendary aura was due to his friendship with the Frozen Mother. In terms of achievements, Ginneas' feats on the battlefield were more than enough for the soldiers who idolized him to wax lyrical for days on end.
     He had once led his soldiers in driving the Hypogeans, spread over the Frozen Prairie, back to the Barred Gate one by one. He used the lessons learned from the Tundra Battle to perfect the Moltenflow Regiment's formation and further reduce casualties. He even devised a new burst hammer, which he personally tested and revised through battle.
     However, even such a legendary figure as Ginneas had to work to earn people's faith.
     A large part of Dwarven behavior was defined by impulsiveness. While it's true that this could explosively unleash their potential in battle, it also meant they often lost their lives unnecessarily.
     Ginneas minimized this sort of senseless sacrifice after he became commander of the Moltenflow Regiment. In the beginning, many impetuous Dwarves accused him of cowardice when he ordered them to retreat. They called him craven, denouncing him for giving up on reclaiming their homeland and sullying the name of commander.
     But in the hundreds of battles which followed, he won countless victories for his countrymen with minimal casualties, enabling even more soldiers to bring their strength to the next battle.
     Now, even support troops who saw no front-line fighting understood the thinking of their unique commander:
     Ginneas was not afraid to fight or die, and never thought to abandon his homeland. He only wished to make every single soldier's sacrifice worth it.
 
     Moonlight suffused the Frozen Prairie with a hazy pale glow, as a group of dark figures was roused by the distant clamor of the Moltenflow Regiment. They swept across the prairie, the cold wind of their passage kicking up eddies of snow on the ground, leaving a conspicuous trail.
     "We finally made it." Ginneas said, observing the area for a long time. Seeing that all was as expected, he smoothed his windswept beard and revealed an excited smile.
     He turned, slung his burst hammer over his shoulder, and laughed heartily: "Alright, boys! Let's send these blasted brutes back home!"
     His soldiers, still happily jostling, fell into formation in the blink of an eye. Each of them brandished their weapon and let out a bloodthirsty battle cry.
     When the idiotic Hypogeans decided on their foolish midnight raid, they fell straight into the trap which Ginneas had laid for them.
     Perhaps they were overconfident in their ability to attack at night, thanks to many previous successes. Unfortunately for them, this time they were up against Dwarves who never backed down, and were always well prepared.
     As the war horn sounded, the brave soldiers of the Moltenflow Regiment advanced towards the dense, dark cluster of Hypogeans, as unstoppable as charging iron chariots. Amidst the thunderous battlecries once again rose an unknown voice, singing the ballad, and once again more joined. The song rolled out loud and clear across the mountains, across the Frozen Prairie, all the way to the remote Dwarven stronghold of Maldan—
     "Moltenflow soul burns in the heart, restless and fitful for winter's revival. Over the majestic mountains, over the peaceful plains, the soil of my homeland lies before me."

163.Name: Summer
163.Story:
The blazing sun shines through the tiny gaps between dense leaves, with spots of light and shadow dancing on Daemia's immaculate arm. She is turning one of her feathers into a miniature messenger. In days, the messenger will travel from this scorching beach on the warm monsoon wind, flying straight to the icy mountaintops until it lands on the shoulder of Titus' who is the guardian of Dura Temple.
    "Everything is fine and dandy this year. The people are enthusiastic and friendly, praising the beautiful sunlight I bring… Soon, we shall meet again." Daemia gazes as her miniature messenger flies off while ships ply the sea in the near distance.
    Each year, she sends out her messenger to Titus, but she is always reluctant to tell him that the mortals are in fact a pitiful species.
 
    Thousands of years ago, Daemia often sent Dura off from the mountaintops and only reunited with her upon her return. Each time, Daemia would decorate the snowy white temple with glorious sunlight and brilliant flowers.
    Daemia had never heeded the mortals whom Dura had looked after. Little did she expect, however, that the people would dream of becoming equals with the gods after Dura had granted them fire. She expected even less that when the mortals finally reaped what they had sown, Dura would perish due to her dwindling power.
    Sad and confused, Daemia decided to leave the mountaintops and take a look for herself the mortal world for which Dura had sacrificed her life.
    Before her departure, Daemia went to Dura's Temple. Titus, the temple's guardian asked a favor of her, that she would share with him what she saw beyond the mountains.
    In the ensuing millennia, Daemia traveled the length and breadth of the various realms of Esperia.
    Daemia brought summer to farmers who had hoped for abundant yields; but in return, she also heard them cursing the droughts. She also granted the gardeners their wish for lush blooms; but soon they started blaming the sudden rain. The nobility who had taken off their fur coats detested the sweltering heat, and even children that were catching fireflies would complain of the sounds of cicadas…
    Experiencing this again and again, Daemia grew used to the mortals' ignorance, greed, rudeness, and lack of gratitude. But she felt sorry for Dura.
    Oh well, let's end it here then. Daemia decided to wrap up her journey and boarded a three-masted ship bound for Hathor from this port, preparing for her return to the mountaintops.
 
    Daemia stood on the deck and gazed into the distance. The wind was strong, the ship was in full sail, and the sailors were singing tunes celebrating summer. "In about two hours," Daemia thought, "the sailors would start feeling the intense heat and cursing summer."
    At this moment, a thick fog rolled over and engulfed the ship in a haze of white. The sailor stopped singing and awaited their captain's instructions.
    Suddenly, a horn sounded in the air. Daemia looked toward the source and saw some sea-dwelling Ya emerging from the water surface. Some of these Ya from the Otter Clan were blowing conches while others were waving flags woven out of aquatic plants, as though they were sending a message to this lost ship.
    Just as she wanted to ask the sailor next to her, Daemia already saw the answer.
    It was a giant chunk of drift ice.
    Ordinarily, drift ice should not appear on this route. The only possible explanation was that the intense heat had melted icebergs far away and sent ice adrift to the middle of the sail route. To make matters worse, a thick fog had descended and blocked the ship's view.
    The captain quickly ordered the chief mate and sailors to control the rudder and sails in order to change the ship's course. However, a three-masted ship was no small boat which could be easily turned around. The crew only had little room to maneuver the ship.
    The clock was ticking and the monsoon wind continued to push the ship forward.
    If nothing was done, the ship would inevitably crash into the ice and break asunder, and over 200 souls on board couldn't be rescued. Their lives hang by a thread.
    Nonetheless, turning the ship too abruptly would also ram it into the Reef Village––the ship might be able to continue sailing after the damage, but around half of the crew could drown. Moreover, it would also wipe out the Otter Clan who dwelt in the village. Besides… the Ya were just doing their best to warn the ship of the incoming hazard.
    Should they try to save as many crew as possible, or should they embrace their horrible fate and avoid putting innocent lives in harm's way?
    Panicked, everyone was staring at the captain's hands which were grasping the rudder tightly.
    "This damn summer wind!" Tears of despair trickled down the captain's face. Obviously, he would have forgotten now the smooth sail they had enjoyed earlier from the wind. At this moment, all he had were curses born out of fear and helplessness.
    Suddenly, Daemia understood Dura's predicament.
    The mortals, who look forward to yet resent summer, are like the captain now who is torn between two choices that would both lead to death. They are not strong enough to pay the price for their choices––unable to withstand droughts on their wheat fields and sudden rain destroying their flowers; unable to fully embrace summer. This was not greed or ignorance. It was simply weakness and frailness.
    And Dura knew that about them. So she expected little.
    Daemia heaved a long sigh and a hot beam shot out from her staff. A powerful gust of wind tilted the ship to a different direction and the sea waves rolled. For a while, the sails creaked and swayed and the ship wobbled violently before it finally skirted the ice and moved toward safer waters.
 
    A year later, Daemia's messenger took off on its journey once again.
    "In the past year, we've been to many places. The land is fertile and nature is vibrant, except that the mortals are clumsy and hard to teach… I reckon, we will only meet in a few hundred years…"
