213.Name: Daughter
213.Story:
By her sixth year at the Violet Orphanage, Mira could barely recall what her old home looked like.
    When she first arrived, everyone told her that Violet Manor was a sanctuary for children with nowhere else to go. It had beautiful gardens, kind caretakers, and friendly playmates. At dinner, everyone would gather around the long table, sharing meals and whispering hopes for the future.
    Back then, Mira naively believed this was the home she'd always dreamed of.
    But the truth was far darker. Beneath its warm surface, the orphanage hid a chilling reality. The "garden" was a training ground for children with unusual abilities; the "kind caretakers" were agents following the orders of shadowy figures; and the "friendly playmates" lived by the law of the jungle, clawing for survival.
    Mira quickly became one of the weak, a target for the stronger children. She had no special power, only an ancient mirror left by her mother—a family heirloom said to connect the living with the world of the dead.
    The only person who showed her kindness was Number 095, though Mira preferred to call her Isabella.
    Isabella taught Mira how to tap into the power of the Graveborn world and helped her escape when the others turned on her. Even when Mira failed to hear the whispers of the Graveborns, Isabella would reassure her, telling her to take her time.
    Sometimes, they talked about the past. When Isabella spoke of her sister, Mira couldn't help but feel a pang of envy. The warmth of a family felt beyond her grasp, a feeling she could barely imagine. Isabella, though, was certain her sister would come for her one day and take her away from this nightmare.

    Mira could only dream about that day, wondering if she, too, might one day find a place in such a loving family.
    But everything changed when an explosion tore through Violet Manor, reducing it to rubble. In the chaos, Mira was separated from Isabella. As her mother's mirror crashed to the ground, cracks webbed across its surface, and a suffocating wave of darkness overwhelmed her.
    It was then that the whispers of the Graveborns finally reached her, and the realm of death claimed her as its own. But when Mira emerged from the ruins, she caught a glimpse of herself in the mirror.
    Her hair was pale, her skin ghostly, and her eyes hollow. She was no longer human.

    At first, she relished in her newfound freedom, wandering through the ruins and into the world beyond, searching for any trace of Isabella. But when she reached the nearest town, the people recoiled in horror. 
    "A Graveborn! How did it get here?!"
    "Alert the Temple of Light!"
    Their screams and panicked cries were a harsh reminder that she didn't belong among them.
    Mira fled, biting her lip to hold back tears. Though she had escaped the prison of Violet Manor, she was still trapped—this time by her own isolation. Her mother's mirror had brought her back, but it couldn't give her a home or a place where she belonged.

    It wasn't long before the forces behind the Violet Orphanage found her. Even in ruins, the organization was still active, and Mira now had to evade both the Temple of Light and her past tormentors.
    She soon realized that the very mirror that made her a Graveborn could also reveal her deepest desires, letting her appear human again. She learned to disguise herself, to walk among the living as the little girl she once was. But it was only a mask, a fragile illusion. Whenever someone showed her kindness, it crumbled the moment they discovered her secret, their warmth turning to fear and disgust.
    Mira grew used to her solitary existence. She moved through the world in her human guise, careful never to let anyone too close. It was a lonely way to live, but it kept her safe. Year after year, she drifted from town to town, never staying long. When the nights grew quiet, her thoughts often turned to her mother and Isabella. She wondered if Isabella had survived the explosion, or if she had finally found her sister. But those thoughts always ended with a sigh, lost to the darkness.
 
    Another Midwinter Festival came, and this year the celebrations were especially lively. Maybe it was because the Hypogean War had ended, but the air was filled with laughter and joy. The festive scenes reminded Mira of her days at Violet Manor—a place of shadows, yes, but also the only place where someone like Isabella had cared enough to talk to her.
    The warmth of the festivities drew her in, but she kept her distance, hiding in the tall grass by the roadside. Years of wandering had made her wary. She didn't want to ruin the joy of the season or risk being discovered and sent running again.
    But then, footsteps broke the silence. Mira's heart leapt into her throat. Before she could slip away, someone pushed away the grass and found her.
    Startled, Mira looked up into a pair of bright, curious eyes. The girl who found her seemed surprised at first, but it quickly softened into a warm smile. "Hey, don't be scared. What's your name? Are you lost?"
    Mira couldn't find her voice. She shook her head quickly, her chest tight with fear. The girl introduced herself as Estrilda and reached out to take Mira's hand. Her touch was warm, so warm that Mira almost forgot to breathe.
    "Well, kiddo, would you like to stay with us for a while?"
    Mira's heart raced, torn between the longing to escape her loneliness and the fear of being rejected. She wanted to trust, but the scars of her past held her back.
    Yet, as she looked into Estrilda's kind eyes, she saw something familiar... a gentleness that reminded her of Isabella. Maybe, just maybe, that was enough to let her believe in someone again.
    Mira's gaze wavered as she met Estrilda's gentle smile. Finally, she nodded, letting the girl's hand guide her as she took her first step toward a new life beneath the falling snow.
    Though she still couldn't bring herself to reveal her secret, deep down, she began to dream of a day when she could live without hiding, when she could be truly accepted for who she was.
213.DisplayTips: Mage. Continuously turns enemies into prisoners, and allies gain combat advantages over prisoners.

217.Name: Marcille
217.Story:
Marcille is a half-elf who plays an active role in Laios' party. She wields Ambrosia, a staff crafted from the roots of second-generation clones of the world tree. Marcille also takes special care of her hair. Her long hair plays a vital role in channeling magic, therefore she changes hairstyles frequently.
    Although Marcille appears to excel in offensive magic, in reality, she researches ancient magic, which is considered taboo. Marcille was a prodigy at the magic school before joining the party, but after witnessing the true nature of the dungeon, she joined Laios' party in the hopes that she could transform the place into a safe zone for gathering magical ingredients.
    With an exceedingly long lifespan and a deep understanding of the magic of nature, Marcille is serious, honest, and slightly neurotic—but only to an adorable degree. Marcille opposes eating monsters, but she has come to realize that monster cuisine is not so bad, leaving her constantly conflicted.
217.DisplayTips: Mage. Requires continuous access to Arcana to maintain her high damage output. Uses the enemy's summons to deal extra damage.

218.Name: Laios
218.Story:
Laios is a tall-man warrior who leads a party of dungeon adventurers, and he excels at mimicking the sounds of a dog to frighten monsters. He prefers using a sword inhabited by a monster called "Kensuke".
    Laios is extremely knowledgeable about monsters, but he's sometimes bad at reading the room. Laios puts his monster knowledge to great use as he and his party of dungeon companions overcome numerous difficulties.
    In a toilsome adventure, Laios set out on a dungeon quest to rescue his younger sister Falin, who had been eaten by a Red Dragon, making use of his knowledge of monster cuisine to sustain his party all the while. His companions were unnerved by this at first, but Laios eventually earned their trust and support and gained a great deal of hands-on experience while gaining a wealth of knowledge about monster cuisine along the way.
218.DisplayTips: Warrior. Uses cooking to provide allies with a variety of support effects and uses his Ultimate to control enemies in front of him for long periods of time.

224.Name: Darklord
224.Story:
E-Rank Hunter.
    Once mocked as "humanity's weakest weapon", Sung Jinwoo never gave up. Despite awakening with the lowest possible rank, he took on dungeon after dungeon to support his ailing mother and younger sister still in school.
    During the Double Dungeon incident, he gained the rare power to level up—growing stronger through quests and slaying monsters. With this power, he began his rise from the weakest to the strongest.
    His strength soared, and after completing a class advancement quest, he became the "Shadow Monarch", a hunter capable of turning fallen monsters into loyal "shadow soldiers".
 
    "What doesn't kill me, makes me stronger."
224.DisplayTips: Ranger. Possesses the ability to level up during battle, constantly growing stronger without relying on others.

225.Name: Lighthunter
225.Story:
S-Rank Hunter.
    Cha Hae-in serves as the Vice-Guild Master of the Hunters Guild.
    She possesses an acute sense of smell that allows her to detect mana power. It was this gift that drew her attention to Sung Jinwoo, whose scent differed from any other hunter she'd ever encountered.
    On the battlefield, she wields a one-handed sword, darting across the frontlines with elegant strikes—her "sword dance" a mesmerizing yet lethal spectacle.
    Though she often seems distant, when her team is in danger or the world faces a crisis, Cha Hae-in never hesitates to step forward. She's a powerhouse on any team—strong, swift, and utterly dependable.
 
    "My blade bows to no fear."
225.DisplayTips: Warrior. Known for dealing divine damage and helping her team overcome "ultimate bosses".

227.Name: OrcAngler
227.Story:
"Hey! Talimar, your fish! Some bird just snatched it!" Gorren shouted, while Ram beside him waved his arms wildly.
    The bird, a silver streak in the air, beat its wings furiously with the fish clamped in its beak. The fishing line went taut, trembling as if it might snap at any second. Yet even in that tense moment, Talimar stayed calm. "Don't worry, Gorren. The line's still holding—"
    She pulled hard in the bird's direction, then quickly reeled in and jerked the rod the other way. In the few seconds the bird reeled from the sudden shift, she seized it right into her hands.
    Gorren, eyes wide, broke into applause. "What skill! Looks like you've done that a thousand times."
    "Plenty more than that," Talimar said with a smile. The bird, struggling in her grip, hadn't taken the hook—only the fish, clamped in its beak with the same desperate strength she once used to cling to life. She unhooked the line and let it go. The gray shape shot low over the water and vanished into the horizon. 
    "Plenty more, huh..." Gorren watched the direction the bird had flown. "Sounds like you've been through a lot. Think you could tell Ram and me about it tonight over grilled fish?"
    "Sure!" Talimar tested her line, baited the hook, and cast again. "But first, we need to catch something worth cooking."
    That night, Gorren finally heard Talimar's tale. But the way she told it was so casual that even famine, in her voice, sounded ordinary. For now, let's leave her words aside and see what truly happened.
    Talimar's homeland lay in the most barren part of the Scorched Expanse, where the most precious thing of all was water. A single pool could keep a family alive, while a river could sustain a whole clan. She was born between rain and sand, raised by the short-lived summer river that flowed past her door.
    In summer, she'd watch the clear water lap over her toes, the fish breaking the surface in little bursts of bubbles. After the rains, termites would crawl from the soil, beginning their great mating flight. Migrating birds swooped down to feast, wings flashing as they darted through the swarm. Even here, in this harsh and empty land, life bloomed fiercely. In winter, she'd stand on dry earth, staring out at endless yellow dunes, the wind's coarse howl in her ears. She crossed the bare riverbed, stepping over smooth stones, as the scent of salty fish soup curled through the bitter wind, mingling with the murmur of familiar voices.
    That river was the clan's lifeline. It brought fish, nourished the soil on both banks, and gave the people a place to put down roots. The fish came only in the rainy season, so the clan perfected the art of catching and drying them for the long, lean winter. They knew the bait fish loved most, the best spots to cast nets, the tools that caught the biggest haul—but none could match Talimar, the girl who could reel in a whole pond with nothing but a single rod. Whenever the clan praised her skill, her father would straighten his back, offering modest words—"Oh, it's nothing"—while his pride swelled clear as day. Talimar never kept her methods secret, but advice like "feel the wind before you cast" and "sense the water's heartbeat as you reel" left even her father puzzled.
    Still, the barren ground couldn't grow strong roots, and the fragile peace was broken before long.
    Talimar was the first to notice something was wrong. The fish in the river were disappearing, and the air carried the harsh scent of swirling sand. The wind whipped dust into the yard, covering the crops' rough leaves with a layer of dry, yellow grit. Overhead, migratory birds called out in harsh voices, warning of what was coming.
    The rains grew scarcer, and the few green shoots in the fields began to wither and turn brown until all life was gone. Without water, the riverbed lay bare. Dust-covered stones baked under the scorching sun, seeming ready to crack. The clan rationed their stored food while searching for new sources. Old dried fish, brittle stalks of grass, insects from the earth, gritty sand... anything that could quiet the hunger gave a glimmer of hope.
    In this drought, the old and the young were the first to fall. The clan buried them beneath the riverbed, piling stones into cairns. These were both a ceremony to honor the dead and a silent pact among the living—to use everything they had, and survive.
    As Talimar stacked stones for her father's cairn, the grief was so deep it almost drowned out her hunger, but she couldn't afford to let tears fall. Lifting her head to hold them back, she saw wintering birds overhead, their harsh cries like a mournful dirge. Just watching them fly made her mouth water, and she longed to become a hawk and snatch them with one bite. Hunger clouded her thoughts, but Talimar's craving pushed her hand toward the fishing rod. Hooks flew through the air, scattering the birds, and exhaustion hit her. Finally, she calmed herself—without bait, there was nothing to catch. She dug into the hardened earth, letting the sharp grit cut her skin, and dug up the termites beneath.
    Using termites as bait and the sky as her river, Talimar's survival instinct finally reeled in a bird. She stared at the struggling creature in her palm. The warmth of its body broke her resolve, and tears finally fell.
    Talimar shared her bird-fishing technique with the others, and for the first time in a long while, pale, gaunt faces brightened with smiles. They raised their rods, holding onto this last hope. Thousands of migratory birds helped the clan endure a grueling year but the awaited rains never came. At last, they realized the land was saying goodbye.
    "Let's go. Only by surviving can we have a home," the clan said, packing their belongings in search of a new life.
    By the old riverbank, Talimar piled a giant cairn, bidding a final farewell to the land that had raised her.
    "If we're leaving, let's go farther," she decided, carrying her beloved fishing rod and walking in the opposite direction of her clan. Alone, Talimar set out to explore every waterway in Esperia, to catch all kinds of big fish and track down all kinds of birds.
    "First stop... the sea the cook once told me about."
    She hummed a childhood tune as she strode into the sunset.
227.DisplayTips: Mauler Support. Works with her fishy companion Baitsy to buff allies and weaken foes.

230.Name: Selene
230.Story:
In Esperia, many marvel at the heavens, dazzled by the glittering stars, while few spare a glance for the quiet light of the moon.
    Though it lacks the stars' fierce glow, it never falters, keeping silent watch in the loneliest of hours.
    And Selene is that moonlight made flesh.
    Some say she was born from the sorrow and prayers of mortals, a goddess claimed by neither dawn nor shadow, but by those who yearn for a single ray of light in the depths of night. She never bends fate, never interferes. Silent, she simply shines, her moonlight brushing across the tears of orphans, the resolve of soldiers, and the stillness of the old.
    For the truly sorrowful never cry out. They simply lift their eyes to the moon, and in that instant, she answers.

    Through the darkness of night, she walks beside many lonely souls.
    In a remote town, a girl who lost her parents sat by the window each evening, pouring her grief to the moon, the only listener she had left. One night, moonlight slipped into her room like gauze, and in her dreams she glimpsed a gentle woman sitting at her bedside. From then on, that silver figure came to her in the night, whispering words of comfort, until the girl learned to smile again.
    On a war-torn frontier, soldiers prayed to the moon for their lovers waiting far away. When moonlight spilled over the battlefield, even in their darkest hour, they remembered their beloveds smile and found the strength to endure. When the war finally ended, they embraced beneath the moonlight, quietly thanking the guardian who had kept watch.
    By a desolate shore, an aging lighthouse keeper had lost track of how long he had kept watch. He spoke to the moon night after night, and the moon listened in silence until his final breath. That night, she lit one last soft gleam to guide his soul toward peace.

    Such was Selene—always watching over the helpless, asking nothing in return.
    But endless vigil wears heavy on even the heart of a goddess. She came to realize that mortals thought of her only in sorrow, as if her very being existed only for tears and silence. Their truest feelings shone at night, yet once day returned, they rushed toward the sun, leaving her light to fade quietly into the sky.
    Her radiance dimmed and her heart sank into voiceless tides. She ceased answering prayers, slipping into the shadows of night to escape the clamor that was never meant for her. Perhaps her light was never that important. Perhaps the world never truly needed her.

    Until she heard those familiar voices again.
    The girl, grown now, still spoke softly to the moon, telling her how happy she was because in her darkest days, a gentle light had walked beside her. The soldier and his lover, reunited, still gazed skyward on clear nights, grateful for the courage moonlight once gave them. On the coast, villagers lit candles at the lighthouse's base, offering blessings to the lonely keeper and praying for his peace across the waters.
    The tender voices layered one upon another, easing her doubt. And in that moment, Selene realized she had never been forgotten. Her glow returned to the night, shining once more for all who still sought her glow.

    Yet as she grew bright again, her heart felt a sorrow unlike any she had ever known.
    It was a broken prayer... blurred, distant, born of some far shore. Its rhythm was strange, its emotions tangled with terror, despair, and a desperate struggle woven together. Selene tried to send her light in answer, but struck an invisible wall. Her radiance shattered against it, swallowed by a widening rift.
    Following the cry, she gazed deep into the current of time—and saw an Esperia both achingly familiar and utterly changed. The mountains stood and the stars wheeled, but at unseen junctures, destiny had slipped, as if nudged just a hair off-course. A long fissure split across the world like ice breaking in winter, and from it seeped thick shadows, spreading through the seams of reality.
    The faces she knew were there, yet their eyes no longer shone. They held only coldness, regret, chaos, and denial. It was a world stripped of redemption, where no one was truly saved, and no one dared even hope for light.

    Selene felt powerless.
    She couldn't cross the rift, couldn't speak in the name of the divine, couldn't even let them feel her presence. All she could do was linger at the edge where two rivers of time brushed past one another, scattering a fleeting gleam into their dreams. A light that might fade in an instant... but a light nonetheless.
    Day after day, she kept watch over the familiar lands of Esperia, even as she lingered by the edge of that fissure, quietly casting moonlight into the chaos beyond. Perhaps the darkness would never answer, but still, stubbornly, she lit her glow against it.
    And at last, within that silence, she sensed the faintest reply. Not words, not prayers—only a glance lifted toward the night sky, a weary traveler pausing mid-step, a child raising tear-brimmed eyes.
    In that instant, Selene understood: even if she could never truly reach across, some souls still felt her. So long as sorrow looked skyward, even for a heartbeat, moonlight would always answer.

    But she wasn't the only one watching this world.
    Two vast wills lingered at the far edge of the rift, their gazes sharp as blades forged from time itself, coldly weighing the branching current of fate. Selene knew their names—Orthros and Zolrath.
    Her heart tightened.
    Until now she had thought the rift was mere accident, a fracture spilling sorrow, a wound dripping shadows from some other world. Yet seeing those two, whose hands had all but molded time itself, she felt a flare of anger.
    Could it be that all of this was nothing more than their game, an endless cycle of tearing apart and stitching back the flow of time? That the prayers she answered with such care were mere illusions in a story they had written?
    She couldn't accept that the world she wept for was only a chessboard, or that the loneliness in those eyes was nothing more than lines in some cosmic script.

    Her glow slowly dimmed as she tried to turn from the fissure... only to feel something deeper still.
    It was no Celestial, no Hypogean. A presence without voice or form, vast and silent, as though it stood on a higher plane, watching from beyond. Its gaze encompassed not only her, but Orthros and Zolrath as well, folding them all within its sight. A chill stole through her, yet just as swiftly as it came, the gaze withdrew, vanishing as if it had sensed her notice and slipped away.
    For the first time, Selene felt true fear. A will beyond even time itself was cutting open a deeper wound.
    She lingered in silence, doubts heavy within her. Yet at last she raised her hand, sending out a thin thread of moonlight, letting it drift into that broken seam.
    She might never grasp the truth of this world's fracture. She couldn't halt the struggles of Celestials, Hypogeans, or whatever lay beyond. But still, she knew the souls living within were real. Their grief, their joy, their whispered prayers were no different from the Esperia she had always guarded.

    She was only moonlight, a quiet sentinel of sleeping worlds. She served no master, promised no miracles. She simply answered the voiceless pleas of sorrow.
    And so, even across the greatest distance, so long as one soul still lifts their eyes to the night, her light will rise. A single, gentle gleam, belonging only to them.
230.DisplayTips: Mage. Advances Lunar Phases via frequent skill usage within the team. During the Full Moon, unleashes a powerful finishing move to damage enemies.

236.Name: Opman
236.Story:
The man who became a hero for fun—Saitama.
    Years ago, while job hunting, he rescued a child from a monster's clutches. In that moment, he rekindled his childhood dream and vowed to become a hero. After three years of intense training, he gained unbeatable strength—enough to fell any enemy with a single punch. But when the life he'd longed for became routine, victory came too easily, and his power felt more like a curse than a gift.
236.DisplayTips: Dimensional Warrior. Generates Interest for allies and enemies during battle, protecting allies while defeating enemies based on Interest levels.

237.Name: Gtornado
237.Story:
Superhuman, an S-class hero with incredible psychic abilities.
    Though arrogant and short-tempered, she wields her powers with precision in battle, overwhelming her enemies with sheer force. Her unmatched strength and confidence earned her the title "Terrible Tornado" from the Hero Association.
    The association relies on her as one of its top fighters, and despite her girlish looks, she's a grown woman and the older sister of the B-Class hero known as "Hellish Blizzard."
237.DisplayTips: Dimensional Mage. Gathers Psychic Power during battle and uses it to strengthen herself and allies.

242.Name: LadyDracula
242.Story:
On that forgotten land, the Carpathian Mountains rose like black spines on the earth, tearing the sky into fragments in the gloomy twilight.
    I, Jonathan Harker, now stand in the shadow of the towering castle. As a legal practitioner, I have come to handle the property matters for its owner. I was greeted by a noblewoman in a deep red velvet gown, who introduced herself as "Dracula," a Countess of Transylvania.
    Never had anyone described to me such a chilling beauty: her skin pale as wax, her figure full and lush, her eyes lowered, and her crimson lips so striking they almost shocked the senses, glistening with a faint moisture as if she had just sipped fresh blood.
    "Welcome to my manor, Mr. Harker," she chuckled with an ancient accent. "Please, enjoy the tranquility here."
    When her cold fingers touched me, a chill ran up my veins and straight to my heart, making me shudder. It was not the warmth of a living person, but the chill of soil from deep within a grave.
    After the work was done, she insisted that I stay a few more days, claiming that certain legal details of the estate still needed to be finalized. But as days passed, I began to realize that there were no servants anywhere in the castle, and still lavish meals would appear out of nowhere late at night. What terrified me most was that when I tried to explore the boundaries of this castle, I found every gate to the outside world locked. Even when I climbed the tower in desperation to look beyond the walls, I only saw bottomless cliffs isolating the castle from the world.
    There was no way out here, save for the iron door bolted shut and the cliff that drops into the abyss.
    I once tried to send a letter to my fiancée Mina, but the Countess smiled and took it from me. The way she looked at me was like one might regard a canary in a cage. "Mr. Harker, the roads are treacherous at night. I would not want any misfortune to befall my guest."
    And so the castle became a luxurious cage. I never once saw the Countess eat, except at night. But whenever darkness fell, howls of wolves echoed from outside the windows, as if paying homage to her.
    I still remember the warning she left me on the night I arrived. "Mr. Harker, whatever happens, do not fall asleep in any room other than your bedroom. This castle has its own rules, and they are not kind to outsiders."
    Until that night, the anxiety of prolonged captivity and my desperate yearning to find an escape drove me to break the warning. I fell asleep in a dusty side hall. At the edge of a hazy nightmare, I saw them.
    Three youths of striking beauty approached me, their pale skin and crimson lips betraying their true nature. The blonde one leaned down and whispered to me: "You are mine..."
    I could feel the scent of sweet blood and decay on his breath. His fangs glimmered coldly in the moonlight, aimed straight at my neck. My body went rigid, as if gripped by an invisible hand, caught between terror and a perverse, intoxicating fascination.
    "Begone!"
    With a sharp command, the Countess emerged from the shadows. She seized the youth by the throat and hurled him against the wall as if he were a rag doll.
    "He is my guest!" she roared, her elegant mask shattering in an instant to reveal the predator beneath. "This man belongs to me!"
    "You always claim the finest prey for yourself, Mother..." The youth rose from the ground, a mixture of mockery and reverence curling at the corners of his mouth.
    She tossed a heavy sack from behind her, inside which something alive seemed to be writhing and emitting faint cries. I shut my eyes, not daring to witness the tragedy that would follow, only hearing the bone-chilling sounds of chewing and beast-like growls.
    At that moment, I finally understood that they were not human.
    The next morning, through eavesdropping, I learned that she had departed by carriage for the port, bound for London. This meant that only I remained in the castle with the three ravenous fiends. When night fell, they would surely break through the doors.
    I had no choice. I had to escape, even if it meant falling to my death over the cliff, it was still better than being devoured by those fiends.
    So I pushed open the tower window, revealing a thousand-foot abyss below. The only way out was to climb down the vertical cliff. I swung myself out, my fingers digging into the weathered stone cracks, my nails splitting and bleeding, staining the gray rock red. With every inch I descended, I was gambling with death. The fierce wind tried to tear me into the ravine, but my fear of those red eyes drove me onward.
    Finally, just as my strength was about to give out, I plunged into the cold, rushing river at the bottom of the ravine.
 
    Time piled up like layers of rotting leaves. Though I miraculously survived the icy river and spent weeks in a monastery in Budapest, returning to the civilized world weakened and terrified, the shadow had not lifted. Instead, it spread like a plague to London.
    It was a ghost ship, laden with death, crashing onto the shores of Whitby.
    It was Countess Dracula. She had come at last.
    She purchased a mansion in the city center, transforming into the deadliest poison in the mist, corrupting the city with a secretive and proud demeanor.
    The first victim was Mina's dear friend, Lucy. That girl who once shone like sunshine was now visibly withering.
    And Professor Abraham Van Helsing, as an expert specializing in the undead, his arrival confirmed our deepest fears.
    The elderly scholar's eyes gleamed with reason as he looked at the two tiny, pinprick red marks on Lucy's neck. He whispered with grave sorrow, "These are the devil's marks, the curse of the undead..."
    Every night, Lucy struggled in her nightmares. She spoke of a beautiful woman calling to her from the window, a voice like a siren's song, promising eternal life and beauty.
    But things didn't unfold as she wished. On that stormy night, we rushed into Lucy's room. The windows were flung wide open, white curtains dancing wildly in the wind. At her bedside, a tall dark figure was hunched over Lucy.
    It was her, Dracula.
    She turned her head, fresh blood staining her pale jaw and the lace on her chest. She smiled at us menacingly, with an unmistakable air of arrogance.
    "The taste of blood is so sweet. Why resist this gift?"
    With a flash of lightning, she transformed into thousands of bats, burst through the window, and vanished into the downpour.
    Lucy ultimately died, or rather, she became something else entirely.
    When we saw her again in the graveyard, Lucy was no longer the gentle girl we knew, but had become a seductive temptress, clutching kidnapped children she intended to feed upon. Professor Van Helsing could only drive a wooden stake through her heart with tears streaming down his face. That piercing scream still echoes in my nightmares.
 
    We became hunters, pursuing the most cunning of "beasts."
    Dracula possessed not only immense power but centuries of cunning. She used mist to conceal her whereabouts and tormented Mina with telepathy... Yes, my beloved was forced to drink her cursed blood. If she were not destroyed, Mina too would become one of the undead.
    We destroyed every coffin Dracula had in London, forcing this noble beast to flee back to her lair. It was a chase across continents, and finally, we returned once more to this cursed land: Transylvania.
    Winter had arrived in full force, with the Carpathian Mountains buried under heavy snow, and fierce winds carrying ice shards that cut into us like knives. Professor Van Helsing, our two companions, and I struggled forward through the blizzard, pursuing the carriage carrying Dracula's last coffin.
    A group of gypsies was escorting her, but even more terrifying were the wolves that followed. Their eerie green eyes flickered through the snowstorm like will-o'-the-wisps.
    "Hurry! The sun is about to set!" Professor Van Helsing shouted hoarsely. "If she lives until sunset, the night will grant her immense power, and none of us will survive!"
    Gunshots echoed fiercely through the canyon as we finally broke through the gypsies' defensive line and drove back the wolf pack with torches and silver bullets. At last, I leaped onto the speeding carriage and struggled with all my might to pry open the heavy coffin lid.
    Just as the last ray of sunset was about to be swallowed by the mountain peaks, the coffin lid was thrown open.
    Dracula lay there, heartbreakingly beautiful. Even in slumber, she radiated a suffocating majesty. Her face resembled a delicate porcelain doll, yet beneath those tightly closed eyes seemed to lurk a thousand years of loneliness and resentment.
    Mina screamed in agony nearby, the curse churning within her.
    I did not hesitate. The curved blade in my hand caught a glint of cold light as I drove it toward her heart.
    Dracula's eyes snapped open, and in that instant, the crimson fury and murderous intent that once burned within them vanished. In their place was an indescribable sense of release and profound sorrow. She gazed toward the sky, as if peering through the heavy clouds to glimpse the sunlight that may once have belonged to a human world centuries ago.
    "Is this... silence?"
    She let out a final, sighing whisper. As the sun fully set, her body began to crumble. The undead form that had once made this continent tremble disintegrated into countless tiny gray particles, like roses reduced to ash, scattering across the vast snowfields.
    In that swirling dust, I witnessed a phenomenon I still cannot explain, nor dare to officially record. Those particles did not settle with the wind, but rose upward, defying gravity, gathering into a brilliant spiral in midair.
    In that instant, the air seemed torn by an invisible force, forming a razor-thin rift. Through the shimmering ripples of strange light, I caught a fleeting glimpse of a sight I had never seen before. It was not a terrifying abyss, but a strange world with a violet sky and verdant forests.
    In that brief glimpse, I seemed to see the ashes coalesce once more, forming new shapes that fell toward that thriving land.
    But this vision vanished instantly. As the last speck of dust disappeared into the rift, everything returned to nothingness.
 
    The wind ceased, and Mina collapsed onto the snow. The red mark on her forehead gradually faded, and she finally regained the essence of humanity.
    The queen of the night had departed, her castle still standing on the cliff like a massive tombstone.
    The legend of the undead had come to an end. For her, this may have been death, or perhaps the beginning of another long journey.
    But in the quiet of the night, when fierce winds rattle the windows, I still think of those crimson eyes. Perhaps in some unknown world, she has found the peace that Transylvania never offered her.
242.DisplayTips: Mage. Collects Blood in her Vampiric Chalice based on her Life Leech to inflict damage and controls on enemies while restoring health to allies.

247.Name: Puppeteer
247.Story:
Judy was a puppet.
    She was kept in a crimson wooden box so confined that she had to crowd together with the other puppets.
    In that sunless cage, every character knew when to take the stage and when to crawl back into the dark.
    So was Judy.
    She was always the first to appear and also the first to be smashed. Each time the curtain rose, she would walk to the stage center and stand still. Before long, the cudgel in Punch's hand would hit hard on her head. The audience would burst into laughter. Judy would fall from the stage, curl back into the box, and wait for the next curtain to rise on the same old scene.
    She had long forgotten how many times she had repeated that suffering performance. The number was vast enough to drive any creature with a soul to madness.
    But Judy didn't have one. She was only a puppet. Punch thought so, too.
 
    Punch was, without question, a shrewd and practiced puppeteer. Punch traveled the market roads with that fine little stage behind him, stopping in town after town to perform. Behind the curtain, he would place the reed in his mouth and produce a voice that was rough and odd. He knew how to work the crowd, especially the children packed into the front row, their eyes shining with an almost fanatical excitement.
    Few had seen Punch's real face. His sign was the smiling puppet on his hand. Over time, everyone forgot there was a performer. Even Punch sometimes did.
    Punch loved the feeling of control. Whenever the cudgel smashed a character's head, he would shout his unchanging final line with pride: "Splendid. The stage deserves nothing less!"
    And under the cold, damp boards of the stage, Judy could hear the applause rolling in, and that arrogant line repeated again and again. She heard every sound. She felt every trace of malice.
    She simply could not speak.
    After the crowd left, Punch would throw the puppets back into the box one by one. The patrolman, the quack doctor, the crocodile, the grim reaper, the devil, and finally Judy.
    Sometimes, before closing the lid, he would look down and stare at her for a while.
    "What are you smiling at?" He said with contempt.
    Judy could not answer. She was only a piece of wood, with an outlandish grin frozen on her face. From any angle, that smile looked wrong, as if she knew something, or as if she were mocking him without a word. It got under Punch's skin. Irritated, he threw her back into the box and snapped the latch shut.
    Darkness swallowed her again.
    In that silence, still enough to drive one mad, Judy kept smiling. She could not move. But her mind began to work without end.
    At first, it was only a slow hatred. Each time the cudgel fell, that cold feeling built and ran deeper. But after so long in the dark, the fury cooled and hardened, until at last it became a bone-chilling clarity.
    She began to study it.
    She could read Punch like an open book. He was nothing more than a mediocre puppeteer. He knew how the patrolman entered, what foolish lines the quack doctor would say, where the grim reaper would raise his scythe, and when to toy with the devil. But the only reason he knew any of this was that the script had not changed in centuries. He simply repeated it by rote, never truly understanding what the play meant.
    The play was never about Punch's cudgel, but the first one to fall. Judy's entrance, Judy's breaking. That was what gave every later cruelty its cue.
    In the box, Judy stripped the play down to its structure. She knew how it worked and its core better than anyone, including Punch.
    Then she began to rearrange it in her mind. If she held the rods, how would she guide the grim reaper's scythe? How would the devil's tricks be undone? How would she make the quack doctor irrelevant before he could speak? Perhaps the patrolman would lose his place on the stage entirely.
    In that tight prison, without spectators, without applause, she rehearsed it all in silence.
    At last, the day came.
 
    It was a usual dusk. Punch went behind the curtain as he always did, placed the reed in his mouth, and took a deep breath.
    "Judy! Dear Judy... it's your turn."
    The strings led her toward the middle of the stage. Her steps were slow. Punch had already lifted the cudgel, waiting for the sound that always followed.
    But this time, before the strike, Judy stopped.
    She stood rooted to the stage, refusing the pull of the strings. Punch jerked them in panic, but her body stayed still.
    Then, she turned around.
    Punch stared. He knew he didn't deliver that command. Yet she was facing him now, that blank smiling face was staring straight through the curtain at the terrified man behind it.
    The audience was becoming restless. They had no idea why the show didn't proceed.
    Then Judy spoke.
    It was not the voice Punch made with his reed. It was a woman's whispering voice, each word sinking into his mind.
    "Punch, did you really think this play was all about you?"
    Punch went rigid. The reed in his mouth burned like heated iron. He nearly screamed.
    "I watched long enough," her voice was flat as still water. "Watched you move the patrolman, toy with the quack doctor, trick the grim reaper, and choke the devil..."
    Outside the curtain, the audience was none the wiser, shifting restlessly as they stared at the silent stage. Losing their patience, someone began to urge the show on.
    "And you," her voice stayed soft, "know only how to break me at the beginning."
    "Every time, I enter first. Every time, I am erased first. And not once did you ask... why me?"
    Punch's hands shook violently.
    "I understand this place better than you ever did." Judy looked at him calmly. "Now it's my turn."
 
    No one could say exactly what happened next.
    Some said that just before the stage collapsed, all the strings drew tight at once and wound themselves around Punch's wrists like ropes turning on their master. Others said the puppet's smiling face cracked open, and what reached out were not splinters, but a woman's hand.
    What the audience remembered was the collapse. The stage seemed to tear open from within. Dust rose in a rush and drove the crowd back.
    When it settled, a woman stood in the ruins.
    With long, slightly disheveled hair, she wore a crimson dress, as if she had only just escaped from some impossibly narrow place. The woman held the control rod tightly in her hand, which had once belonged to Punch.
    At her feet knelt a large and grotesque puppet, its face fixed in Punch's signature wild grin, yet the eyes that should have held life were hollow now, empty as bottomless pits.
    From that day on, the puppeteer was never seen again.
    Only an old glove was found in the ruins. The leather was twisted and shrunk in on itself, as if something inside had fought to get out and at last split it open from within, leaving only a vacant shell behind.
 
    In time, the woman called Judy raised a new stage and traveled with it from town to town. No one knew how many nights it had crossed, or when it had come to Oakenfell. The audience was unfamiliar with this ancient play, and had no way of knowing which long-forgotten theater had first given it life.
    Judy did not mind. The old play had found a new stage. This time, it would open again in a different world.
    The players had not changed. The patrolman, the quack doctor, the crocodile, the grim reaper, and the devil. But their fates had been completely rewritten.
    Whenever the curtain rose, she would send the puppet named "Punch" to the center of the stage and touch its cold shoulder lightly with the control rod. A red light would flash in its eyes, like a struggle born of pain, and like rage being bent into obedience.
    Then the slaughter would unfold as it always had. The patrolman was smashed. The quack doctor was ripped apart. The crocodile, the grim reaper, and the devil were all reduced to pieces in a series of mechanical, brutal movements. Numb to it all, the audience clapped, laughed, as if watching a farce.
    And Judy watched "Punch". Like she once had, he was pulled to center stage by strings and the weight of a script already set. The smile that had once belonged to the old master of the play was now fixed forever on another empty shell.
    "Splendid. The stage deserves nothing less." She lifted the control rod and spoke the old closing line softly.
    Only her voice had quietly become Punch's, and the smile on her face was no different from the one she had worn as a puppet.

251.Name: Athena
251.Story:
"Wisdom is a cold pair of scales suspended from the tip of a spear. It demands that you always find the weightiest counterweight between life and death, destruction and survival."

    From the moment I sprang forth clad in armor and bearing a spear from the head of my father, Zeus, I understood how to preserve the greatest order at the smallest cost. The divine order of Olympus is a vast and intricately woven web, and I am its keeper.
    Until Poseidon's sinful hands brutally tore through that web.
    He came with the sea, reeking of salt and malice, and flooded the white marble steps of my temple. Beneath my own statue, within a sanctuary that belonged to me alone, the God of the Sea destroyed the priestess who had devoted her life to my service. It was an act of arrogant provocation, a mockery of the authority I held over war, bound as I was by the very laws the gods had forged.
    I tightened my grip on the Triumphant Lance. Fury blazed beneath my helm as a divine tempest gathered at its tip, powerful enough to tear the heavens apart.
    But I did not strike.
    The moment the Triumphant Lance fell, it would become an all-out war between the two chief gods. Sea and land would tear each other apart, and in the end, it would be the cities of mortals that bore the fury of the seas and the wrath of the gods.
    The laws of Olympus did not permit a god to shatter the balance that sustained the world for the sake of a single mortal's tragedy. Had I kept her within my temple and openly declared her under my protection, Poseidon would have taken it as a call to war.
    So I stilled the divine tempest, lowered the tip of the Triumphant Lance, and turned it toward the battered girl beneath the altar.
    In the name of "punishment," I laid a curse upon her. I crowned her head with hissing serpents and turned her tear-filled eyes into a gaze that reduced all who met it to stone. That power did indeed protect her, but it also ruined her. It kept those who sought to harm her from meeting her gaze, yet it also kept the innocent from ever drawing near.
    I allowed the world to believe it was the price of sacrilege. I let them drive her from the cities of mortals and brand her a monster. Only then would the gods believe that the order of Olympus remained unbroken.
    I did not save her. I merely gave her the strength to never again be destroyed after she had been ruined.
    I preserved the balance of order, but she alone was the one I abandoned.

    For centuries thereafter, I remained seated upon my throne atop Olympus.
    Beneath the clouds, the Aegean lay like a cold bronze mirror. For centuries, I dared look at her only through its reflection. I forced myself to see only the horror of the Gorgon, convincing myself that the judgment I had passed was not entirely wrong. Yet I could never bring myself to look directly upon the terrible price that scarred that forsaken isle.
    I watched as she turned the mortal heroes who came to slay her into stone. I watched as, with those very stones, she slowly raised upon that desolate shore a ruin in the image of the temple that had once been mine.
    From within those ruins, she would lift her eyes to me across the sea of clouds and the realm of the gods, fixing me with the very gaze that could turn all things to stone. There was hatred in her eyes, but deeper still was a merciless scorn. With those ruins, she was raising an altar to my shame.
    I could not look away.
    She never questioned me. Her very existence was enough to pass judgment on my wisdom, day after day.
    Even if I could free her from the serpents and the petrifying gaze, I could not restore the heroes turned to stone, erase the world's memory of her as a monster, or undo what happened that night. And if I were to take that power from her as well, she would once again become a mortal whom anyone who came for her could harm.
    To leave the curse in place or to lift it would still be another choice I made for her.
    Only then did I understand what I had truly taken from her. It was not only her human form, but also the right to decide her own fate.
    One side of the scales had long since tipped beyond my sight.

    That day, the Three Fates wove the name of Perseus into the end that awaited her.
    I was meant to place the final counterweight upon the scales: to guide the hero to that forsaken isle, to have him use the reflection in his bronze shield to avoid Medusa's gaze, and to strike off her head. Her severed head would be set into the Aegis, while Olympus would celebrate it all as a hero's triumph. For centuries, it had been the most unquestionable judgment I could have made.
    But when she lifted her eyes on that forsaken isle, the hand that held the counterweight could no longer set it down. Reflected in the shield was not the Gorgon, but the priestess who had knelt before my altar and waited for me for centuries.
    Perseus was still crossing the sea. I left him behind, along with the bronze shield and the glory that had been destined for him.
    This time, no hero would ever reach the isle. I raised the Aegis, no longer to carry out the gods' judgment, but simply so she could see that the divine power which had wrought the curse, and the curse itself, at last faced one another upon the same shield.
    The side of the scales that had borne the weight of order for centuries finally came crashing down, beyond everyone's sight.
    A piercing cry split the heavens as a deep fissure tore through the golden vault above. She shattered the ruined altar she had raised in the image of my temple and, without a moment's hesitation, leapt into the abyss beyond.
    For a moment, I almost watched her leave in silence, as I had for centuries. But I knew all too well what that would mean. Silence would be yet another choice made on her behalf, and the judgment I owed her would forever lose its chance to arrive.
    I rose to my feet and cast one last glance at the golden splendor of Olympus. It remained as majestic and unblemished as ever. The gods still sang their praises, as though that night had never come to pass, as though no one had ever knelt beneath my altar to beg me for even the smallest measure of protection.
    In that moment, I grew weary of those cold scales.
    I cast aside the divine robes that embodied the glory of Olympus, tightened my grip on the Triumphant Lance, and raised the Aegis. This time, neither spear nor shield was lifted to preserve the honor of Olympus. They would follow me into the rift beyond the laws of Olympus, to answer the judgment that had been centuries overdue.

252.Name: Medusa
252.Story:
"Stone does not bleed. It was the only mercy Athena ever granted me."
 
    The sea winds that had swept this forsaken isle for centuries still carried the taste of salt and blood. As I slowly passed by the cold, ruined walls, another stone statue came into view, locked in lifeless quiet. Once, he had been a mortal hero who attempted to slay me. Now he stood forever with his sword held aloft, frozen in a charging stance. He had become yet another pillar supporting the dome of this grand hall.
    Centuries have passed, and the statues scattered across this island have long since become too many to count. The temple's foundations, its steps, even its altar are all built from their petrified remains. Some are forever frozen with swords drawn as they charge. Some remain on their knees, pleading for mercy. Others still hold their blades aloft, caught in the attempt to sever my head before the stone claimed them.
    Every single statue is but another soul who tried to define me.
    Monster. Gorgon. Calamity. An abomination whose head had to be taken.
    They burdened me with countless dreadful names, yet no one remembers that before the serpents stirred upon my head, I too once bore a mortal name.
    I remain here, a priestess without a god, wandering these ruins built from heroes turned to stone. The shrine stands empty, and the only thing I continue to worship is the judgment that never came.
 
    I was once the most devoted priestess in Athena's temple. I believed, with all the fervor of my faith, that if I remained pure and devoted all my youth to the goddess, I would live out my mortal life beneath the light of her wisdom.
    That faith endured only until towering waves shattered the gates of the temple. In that moment, everything I had believed in was swept away.
    Poseidon's trident shattered the silence that had long enveloped the temple, and his shadow fell across Athena's altar. It was a struggle for power between the gods, and I was nothing more than a sacrifice the sea had claimed to humiliate wisdom. That night, I knelt before the cold altar and begged the lofty goddess for a single act of true protection.
    But the goddess merely looked down upon me from her pedestal, her gaze filled with pity, yet she said nothing.
    Only after the tide had receded did the curse finally descend upon me.
    She crowned my head with hissing serpents, filled my eyes with the curse that turned all who met my gaze to stone, and took from me even the right to weep. She did not punish Poseidon. The laws of Olympus forbade her from passing judgment on another of the chief gods, and the God of the Sea would have seen any open act of protection as a declaration of war.
    It was all she could give me.
    It wasn't until the first band of marauders set foot on the island and were turned to stone that I finally understood her wisdom. It was never merely a curse. It was the only weapon she could place in my hands after I had been ruined. It ensured that anyone who came for me would first be frozen beneath my gaze.
    That very weapon also took my face, my name, and any hope of ever returning to the world of mortals.
    I could never truly hate her. It was the curse she bestowed upon me that ensured I would never again be at anyone's mercy.
    Yet I can never forgive her. She preserved the order of the gods, leaving me alone to bear the cost. I still live, but only as an object of mortal fear. No one dares meet my gaze, and no one would ever draw near the woman who once bore a mortal name.
    All I can do is remain within this temple of stone, waiting for the judgment that refuses to fall.
    I know she is always watching me from above the clouds. Watching as I lay each shattered piece of my faith upon another, until it becomes stone. Watching the sin she wrought with her own hands weather the ages into a scar this forsaken isle will never lose.
    I will never bring this farce to an end for the gods. I will live on forever as the stain upon her flawless name that can never be washed away.
 
    That was the day the ending they had written for me was finally woven into the threads of fate.
    A hero named Perseus was already crossing the sea. The gods had armed him with a gleaming blade and a polished bronze shield, so he could turn my own gaze against me and take my head without ever looking into my eyes. Even my death had long since been written as another hero's triumph.
    But that blade never reached me.
    I lifted my head and looked to the heavens one last time. For all those centuries, it was never the hero I had been waiting for. I was waiting for her to look back at me just once.
    This time, Athena did not avert her eyes. She raised the Aegis, letting the gaze of my serpent eyes fall upon its golden surface. For centuries, anyone who met my gaze was turned to stone. Yet the one who now returned my gaze was the very goddess who had fashioned these eyes with her own hands. She did not turn to stone. It was not the shield that cracked, but the old vows, the old sins, and the judgment that had been so long denied.
    A piercing cry split the heavens as a deep fissure tore through the golden vault above. Before it, even the threads of the Three Fates lost their course.
    So there was another sky beyond the order she had upheld.
    I shattered the altar built from the petrified heroes, never once looking back, and leapt into the unknown abyss.
    In this new world, I am no longer a priestess bound to any god. I no longer have to bear the burden of their old sins, nor do I need her distant protection anymore.
    They once turned my name into another word for monster. From this day forward, that name belongs to me alone.

1126.Name: AvengerSBane
1126.Story:
"If you could choose, would you pick a wondrous dream, or a spine-chilling nightmare?"
        
        The patient sat before me asked.
        
        Meeting his bloodshot gaze, it was clear his question was asked in all seriousness. But simply saying "a wondrous dream, of course" was becoming increasingly harder to say.
        
        Laughing at himself with a mocking chortle, he began to tell me of his experience.
        <c><line></c>
        
        I live in a far out backwater village, right at the cusp of the Empire. It doesn't have much to do with the rest of the world, but there's enough to get by on. The villagers live a simple life, it's tough, but not so tough that they can't handle it. At least, that was the case until a few months ago...
        
        A few months ago, folks in the village started having nightmares, lots of nightmares. Farmers would see their crops fail and families starve, merchants would see bandits pillaging and raiding. The military veterans who'd served with the Frontier Regiment would see blood-soaked Maulers, cascading over the border and slaughtering the townsfolk... In short, they all dreamed of the things they feared most, the things they didn't want to confront.
        
        In the beginning, folks were a little anxious about it, but found comfort in reassuring themselves that it was mere "coincidence". But then as time went on, the number of folks having nightmares grew, and so did their anxiety. The whole village was enshrouded by a sense of unease.
        
        The Village Head sent for help from the Temple, but the village was so out of the way that getting there and back would take the best part of three months. There was nothing for it, we had to wait.
        
        Things carried on this way for about a week, the entire village plagued by nightmares. Everyone was on edge, their dark-ringed eyes heavy with sleep deprivation, they were afraid to sleep but too exhausted to avoid passing out. Unable to fend off the exhaustion, they would eventually pass out, only to be reawakened by those horrific nightmares.
        
        One night, I slipped into yet another nightmare. However, something about this one was different. A little pink-haired girl with butterfly wings appeared, fluttering around, a shower of magical glittering dust falling through the air as she flew. Whatever the dust covered, the nightmare beneath it seemed to dissolve as if it were snow in the sun.
        
        "Ezizh! I will not permit you to foul people's dreams any longer!"
        
        She yelled out. Opposite her was some sort of demonic creature, it rose from the nightmare that the dust had not yet touched. Its arms had been tied up with vines and an ominous black mist permeated the air around it.
        
        "Go ahead Tasi, try your best."
        
        That was the moment it dawned on me. This demonic thing, a Hypogean called Ezizh, was responsible for the villagers' nightmares. Just before I lost consciousness, the two began to face off against one another.
        
        When I reawakened, the villagers were thrilled, all talking about Tasi and how she appeared in their dreams. Even though the nightmares hadn't gone entirely, there was now a ray of hope for us.
        
        Several days continued in much this way, as Tasi appeared in everyone's dreams and fought fiercely with the Hypogean. The decisive battle happened in my dream, a wondrous dream and a spine-chilling nightmare mingling and alternating. Sometimes I would find myself enveloped in an ocean of flowers, other times a sea of flames. The endless back and forth between dream and nightmare was seemingly going to swallow me, and yet I was fully prepared to be swallowed.
        
        On the brink of losing my grip on the world, Tasi fluttered her wings vigorously, glittering dust gushed forth shattering the stalemate between dream and nightmare. The nightmare was totally dispelled, and the Hypogean fled. The dust spread all around, weaving the most extraordinary dream I'd ever seen... Where once stood desolate, barren wastes, now grew never-wilting blossoms, rivers of fine wine, and a fruitful field of golden wheat. No poverty, no famine, no pestilence to be seen. I saw the Village Head embrace his long deceased wife, I saw the military veteran return to the barracks in perfect health, and I saw the merchant smile as he opened a business in Savannah, greeted by an endless flow of customers.
        
        The very next day, no-one roused from their sleep until after midday. One by one they stepped out, teary-eyed with emotion as last night's incredible dream still lingered. Having awoken from the dream, life could gradually be restored to normal, or so I thought. But truly seeing the impoverished land and run-down village after being immersed in such a beautiful dream left me with a feeling of disappointment.
        
        Three days later, the villagers erected a statue of Tasi, giving up whatever food they had by way of offerings. Passing by it, everyone bowed with reverence, perhaps hoping that Tasi would return and bring everyone another wonderful dream.
        
        A week passed and Tasi did not appear. The food left in offering was reclaimed, and the villagers no longer bowed to the statue.
        
        Another few days went by, and still Tasi didn't appear. The village folk's hopes turned to disappointment, and then unbridled rage. Some even began to curse Tasi under their breath, condemning her selfishness and neglect.
        
        I've no idea who cast the first stone, but one night someone did. By the time the sun rose, the statue had been smashed to pieces.
        
        The villager's desire to return to that beautiful dream didn't wane with the passing of time. Every glance at the barren land and shabby houses swelled their desire to return to their dreams. Eventually, some folks just shut their doors and stayed in bed, hoping beyond hope that the beautiful dream would return. But it never did.
        
        The wheat crops became overgrown with rampant weeds, uncared for by the people. A constant reminder of the difference between dream and reality. The worse reality became, the more we wanted to go back to that beautiful dream. The village folk became increasingly irritable, their desires never being met and the feeling of dissatisfaction welling up. Trivial matters were enough to spark brawls.
        
        Then someone threw the first punch, then a second, and a third... The village descended into chaos. Dazed, it seemed like I could see an eerie dark mist emanating from everyone. Like vines, it climbed and wrapped itself around them, spreading and condensing into a foggy cloud that enshrouded the entire village.
        
        Suddenly, a huge, ghastly mouth appeared from within a void, swallowing the dark mist.
        
        "Nightmares give rise to fear. Beautiful dreams give rise to indulgence..." The Hypogean's words rang true. "The will of mortals is truly fragile and easily broken, but the power of its desire is beyond compare."
        
        The Hypogean's silhouette emerged. It had broken free of its bonds, the huge figure of a beast materializing into something more solid. Tentacles twisted and writhed from its back, reaching out and blotting out the night sky.
        
        Then, I understood. It had never left us. It had allowed itself to be defeated, to make us feel the relief of Tasi's aid, and to feed on our negativity when it was gone. Our negativity had become the sustenance for it to break free and descend into our reality...
        <c><line></c>
        
        "So how did you escape?" I couldn't help asking after hearing all this.
        
        "Tasi." The patient replied, smiling bitterly. "I suppose the Hypogean wasn't quite free of the dream realm yet, when Tasi charged in and both vanished from sight."
        
        "Vanished?"
        
        "Who knows where they went. I don't. Maybe they're still in the dreamworld fighting?" The patient paused a moment before continuing, "I really want to see Tasi again... To thank her in person."
        
        Although the patient's expression conveyed a sense of genuine sincerity, I couldn't help but catch a flash of madness in his bloodshot eyes.

1142.Name: SLG_BOSS_WindMan
1142.Story:
The "Nautical Annals of the Empire" tell of a ferocious storm at the time of Respen's birth. 
        The violent, stormy winds that swept through many coastal towns almost sent everything not bolted down to the ground sailing off into the sky.
        Amidst the mighty roar of the elements, Respen first opened his newborn eyes. Surrounding him in its embrace, the wind gently kissed his forehead and eyes. Converging from every corner of the world, the winds resonated with him, bestowing upon him the ability to feel and know them.
        As he came into the world, the winds picked up dramatically, enormous waves crashed against the Empire's coastline, and even the ancient underwater canyons seemed to tremble to the rhythm of the wind's fury.
        
        As time went on and the storm continued to rage, it seemed only to escalate in severity, putting coastal towns in greater danger. As it's ferocity grew, Khazard, the Guardian of the Tides, arose from the waves before Respen.
        The newborn elemental looked at him. Khazard's eyes were remarkably calm and gentle.
        Respen soon calmed down in the water elemental's soothing embrace. Just like an infant, he clumsily floundered around, gradually discovering his own limbs.
        With Khazard's help, the ferocious storm gradually eased, the coast once again restored to peace.
        Nature's five great elements are all closely related, kept in a state of harmony by the combined efforts of the five elemental Guardians.
        Changes in factors such as temperature and topography influence the ever-present winds. Born of the wind, Respen, too, is influenced by these factors, his personality fickle and volatile.
        Some ocean-bound fleets learned only too well of Respen's temperamental nature as the gentle sea-breeze so quickly became a howling gale that tossed their ships into tumult in all of a split-second. The ships' crews holed up in their cabins prayed fervently that the fickle 'Windchild' would bless them with smooth passage into port.
        
        As well as his eccentric nature, this new elemental Guardian didn't yet seem entirely capable of controlling his powers.
        In order to restore balance to the elements, Khazard took it upon himself to guide Respen, aiding him in reconnecting with the blowing winds each time he lost control.
        The greatest storm is born at sea, and so it is that it shall fade away there, too.
        With Khazard's patient guidance, Respen gradually came to understand his role as an elemental Guardian. He draws back the wind, alters the flow, and eliminates the elemental chaos at the coastline, restoring order to everything.
        As the environment improved, Sankast also gradually flourished. The Golden Coast was bustling with ships of all shapes and sizes, the ocean breeze filling their sails.
        Sankast was awarded the title 'City of a Thousand Sails'. Grateful for Respen's blessings, the people gave thanks to Respen and erected a statue in his honor, calling him The Windchild.
        Just as everything was in proper order, Khazard suddenly vanished.
        Respen couldn't find him.
        He initially believed Khazard had simply returned to nature, since such is the destined end of all elementals. Yet, a new Guardian of the Tides had still not been born.
        Respen felt an insurmountable grief and loneliness at the loss of his mentor. He searched continuously and tirelessly, until one day a peculiar message drifted to him carried by the currents of the wind.
        Following this calamitous essence to the Bastion of the Elements, he found a Hypogean, its heavy breath chilled and biting.
        Splashed by flames of elemental chaos, the Hypogean had broken through, reaching out and touching the enormous Elemental Altar. As the powerful Hypogean made contact with it, Respen could feel the fabric of elemental order within being eroded and torn asunder.
        The Elemental Altar was the foundation of the elements. If it were to be destroyed, the chaos that would ensue would be disastrous for Esperia. The power of the Gods would be depleted even further.
        
        Respen tentatively called out to the figure at the Elemental Altar, "Khazard?" Yelling out loud the name of one once admired by so many.
        Khazard turned around, coldly looking down at him, "Do you intend to stop me, too? Just like them?" His blood-red eyes glared at Respen, his icy grin chilling him to the core.
        Suddenly, Respen clocked the dead bodies of the Wilder Elementalists strewn about the place, surrounding the pair of them.
        "Why are you doing this?" Respen averted his eyes from the corpses, all so clearly cut down with ice. He just couldn't believe it was all real.
        When did all this begin? What on earth drives a faithful elemental Guardian to become a degenerate Hypogean?
        Khazard wasn't remotely interested in answering any questions. "Pitiful worm, I truly wish you could see what I see." 
        The Hypogean's contempt for Respen was evident, he made no attempt to hide it. The ice snake coiled around his arm raised it's head. A sudden blast of ice blocked the pathway as a formidable ice wall rose up from the ground and completely surrounded Respen.
        
        Bound into an unprecedented state of inaction, Respen's Wind Swallow slammed into the ice wall desperately attempting to break through, but the icy cage wouldn't budge.
        
        "Only the power of a hurricane can break my ice cage. You, who have never had full control of your moods and emotions, are still powerless to control the winds. Isn't that so?" Khazard felt his time has been wasted on Respen and lamented it thus, sighing bitterly, "... Such an incompetent Guardian, why not return to nature a little sooner, hmm?"
        
        As Khazard moved, his ice creation moved with him. Respen was suddenly impaled from all sides as his icy prison closed in, cutting deep into his flesh. "What you said before... about the Guardian's duties... Was it all just lies?" The bitter cold was sapping away his will, "I thought...
        
        We could bridge the elements and generations, be teacher and student... or even... friends."
        
        Respen closed his eyes. The anger and betrayal he felt that swirled around his mind suddenly receded like the tides. In his mind's eye he saw a clear image of Khazard, Guardian of the Tides.
        He remembered a magnanimous hand upon his head, crystal clear blue eyes looking down at him, "One day I shall disappear, just like the seafoam. When that day comes, you must remember my words, do not forget... Promise me this."
         ...
         "You are not him." Respen opened his eyes, glaring daggers at the Hypogean before him. "Khazard would never criticize others. He told me I can be anything I want to be, just like the ever changing winds."
        A sudden elemental surge welled up within the ice cage. A split second later, Respen appeared before the Hypogean like a sudden flurry of wind, launching into an unexpected counterattack. 
        "None shall define me... Incompetent or otherwise, it is not for you to decide!"
        ...
        Even in those final moments, Hypogean Khazard still couldn't believe that Respen had broken free of the ice cage and driven him back.
        Because of Respen, the crisis at the Bastion of the Elements was temporarily averted.
        The ocean winds are still treacherous, much like a child throwing a tantrum one moment and giggling with the glee the next.
        
        The citizens of the Thousand Sail city continue to adore their Windchild just as always.
        
        At every festival, they never forgot to present his statue with wreaths of flowers, even though they know he will do whatever he pleases anyway.
        
        He is fickle and unpredictable, making humans fear the awesome power of nature.
        Acting on his own whims, never being confined to rules and changing the landscape. He even changed the way the land is pollinated, inadvertently causing the blooming of flowers all across Esperia, each bringing its own attitude.

1143.Name: SLG_BOSS_Wildkin
1143.Story:
In the days before the unification of the Mauler tribes, the falcon clan were spoken of in fear. Though not particularly numerous, they were well equipped and fierce fighters. There were very few who didn't fear the infamous lightning-fast raids of the winged terrors. They would strike quickly and without warning, ignoring the rivers and hills that would slow anyone else. There was almost no guaranteed refuge from their attacks, no place too remote to escape the reach of their talons. Many lesser tribes were subjugated, their most prized possessions taken away with a beating of wings even before their best warriors had finished bleeding out onto the ground.

    Skriath, however, stood out from his brethren. The militaristic fervor that characterized, and, in his estimation, consumed his people was missing in him. Rather than the spoils of war, it was knowledge that he sought. Every morsel of wisdom was as precious loot for the inquisitive falcon. The stories of the various far-flung peoples his own clan encountered fascinated him, and he would often accompany the warriors on their raids. His aversion to combat, however, did not endear him to his peers. There was never a shortage of derisive remarks about the weakling who would spend time poring over the artifacts and writings of other clans rather than taking their belongings at the point of a blade. As such, Skriath occupied a very low place in his clan's strictly hierarchical structure. He ate scraps and wore rags, and his yurt was in tatters.

    Despite his low status, Skriath was wise. He saw that the path his people were on was one of disaster. They were becoming more reviled with each new moon. The brutal treatment they had meted out on other clans had made them incredibly unpopular, and he knew that eventually they would find it returned to them in kind. He went to the elder and urged him to guide his people in a different direction: a path of peace, enlightenment, and growth. Skriath was roundly castigated without the slightest hesitation. He was denounced, and what few things he owned deemed worth keeping were taken from him. Everything else was destroyed. Before the sun had set, he had taken wing. Now an exile with nothing to his name, he was forgotten by the others the moment he disappeared over the horizon.

    Seasons passed in blood and conflict, and eventually Skriath's warning proved to be well-founded. The many enemies that the falcons had earned over the years banded together. Embittered and hungry for revenge, they tracked down the warlike folk who had brought them so much pain with the intent to not only retrieve that which had been stolen from them, but also to erase from the world those who had stolen it.

    The attack was merciless. The ground was littered with feathers soaked red. Once keen eyes stared blankly at nothing and became pale. The falcons had been surrounded, their advantage of flight negated by rank upon rank of archers that shot down those who tried to escape the slaughter. It seemed that all was lost when a strange banner was seen at the head of an unknown force, charging toward the fray. Combatants on both sides braced themselves, confused at who they faced. The banner bore a mark that had not been seen in decades: the mark of the united Mauler tribes. Indeed, Maulers from nearly every clan made up the column. A falcon led them.

    They smashed into the archers, laying waste to their ranks and making clear their allegiance. The tide of the battle turned swiftly, and as more bodies began to fall the original attackers felt their resolve draining. They began to retreat and surrender. The falcon leading the intervening force shouted a command, and the killing stopped entirely. The three armies stood mixed among each other, weary and wounded. Realization dawned on the beleaguered falcon clan and shock registered on every face. The exile from years ago had become their savior.

    Peace was made. Lands and artifacts long ago taken away were returned. A new era of understanding and cooperation had begun.

"Wisdom will show you the way"
